876.title: Raksha Bandhan
876.hook: a Hindu festival where sisters tie a thread on brothers' wrists, a bond of protection
876.howItsDone: On Raksha Bandhan, Hindu sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists, mark their foreheads and offer sweets, and brothers give gifts and promise their protection; some families also include cousins and close friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Tu B'Av, with borrowed white in the vineyards. Your line was dance in white.

A plate on a small tray: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few grains of rice, a sweet, and a bright thread with a flower of tinsel in the middle. A sister holds it. Her brother sits in front of her, wrist out, a little embarrassed, a little pleased. She marks his forehead, ties the thread, feeds him the sweet. He gives her a gift and a promise. Hindu families who keep the festival, in India and far beyond, share scenes like this one day each year.
screen: `A LAMP, A SWEET, A THREAD.` → `A WRIST HELD OUT.` → `A GIFT AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Raksha means protection, and bandhan means a tie, a bond: the bond of protection. The thread itself is usually called a rakhi. The sister ties it and prays for her brother's wellbeing, and the brother promises to stand by her. Second, the stories behind it. Hindus tell more than one. One, told in the Puranas, the old story collections, has the goddess Indrani tying a protective thread on the wrist of her husband Indra, king of the gods, before a battle. Another, a story people tell about the Mahabharata, has Draupadi tearing a strip from her sari to bind a cut on Krishna's finger, and Krishna, years later, protecting her in her hour of need. These are tradition's stories, told in more than one version, and people tell them for what they mean more than as history. Third, what the thread does. A rakhi is light. It snaps easily. It frays. Nobody is protected by its strength. The protection lives in what it stands for: someone remembered you, someone promised. The thread is the small visible end of a large invisible bond. Fourth, how wide it reaches. Some families tie rakhis between cousins, and between friends who have chosen to be like brother and sister. Some sisters tie them on sisters. Some people send them by mail across oceans. The heart of the day isn't who ties it. It's the promise: I'm on your side, and I'm not going anywhere. This one ties love to a wrist, where it can be seen all day.
screen: `THE BOND OF PROTECTION.` · `INDRANI, DRAUPADI, KRISHNA.` · `A THREAD THAT SNAPS EASILY.` · `HOW WIDE IT REACHES.` · then, large: `RAKSHA BANDHAN.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands palms up and feel the inside of your wrist, where a thread would go, then bring to mind someone who has stood by you, a sibling, a cousin, a friend, anyone who has been family to you, and remember a moment they kept you safe. Hold both of you in mind, as if one thread ran between your wrists, and if you pray, ask for their protection in your own tradition's words.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection, a Hindu festival when a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist and he promises to stand by her. Today's word.
Your line: the thread. The thread is thin; the promise is what holds. That's day eight hundred seventy-six.

877.title: Different loves
877.hook: agape, bhakti, metta, ishq, ren: not one love under many names, but many loves
877.howItsDone: Each tradition keeps its own word: Christians speak of agape, Hindu devotees express bhakti in song and worship, Buddhists practice metta toward all beings, Sufi poets write of ishq, and Confucian teaching roots ren in family duty.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Raksha Bandhan, the bond of protection: a thread tied on a brother's wrist. Your line was the thread.

Five words, from five places. Agape. Bhakti. Metta. Ishq. Ren. A greeting card could print them in a circle around a heart and call them all love, in five languages. A lovely card, and maybe a wrong one. Put them back where they came from, and they pull in different directions. One gives without waiting to be earned. One sings to God. One wishes well to every living being. One burns. One starts at the family table.

Agape first. It's a Greek word the New Testament uses for love, and in First Corinthians the King James Bible renders it charity: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind.” It's love as a gift, and in the Gospels Jesus stretches it as far as the enemy. Agape points outward, to the neighbor and the stranger. Bhakti is Sanskrit. In Hindu devotion it means loving God personally, with the whole heart, and in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the devoted one is dear to him. Bhakti points toward a Beloved with a name and a face. Metta is Pali, from the Buddhist teachings, often put into English as loving-kindness. In the Metta Sutta the image is a mother guarding her only child, and that care is stretched toward all beings, without limit. It asks nothing back. Ishq is a word Sufi poets use for a love that burns and won't stay polite. Rumi calls love the astrolabe of God's mysteries. Ishq points toward the One, and it aches. Ren is Chinese, from Confucius, often rendered humaneness. Asked about it, Confucius answers: love people. And the Analects say being a good son and a good brother is its root. Ren starts at home and grows outward through duties. So here's the turn. These aren't five names for one feeling. They differ in who is loved, what is asked, and where it starts. Metta wishes all beings well; ren begins with your own parents. Bhakti longs for one Beloved; agape reaches the enemy. Each word means most inside its own tradition. One English word flattens them. Keeping them apart is a way of honoring each.

segments.voice: Let the five pass slowly through your mind, like faces in a crowd: agape, the gift that reaches the stranger; bhakti, devotion to the divine; metta, goodwill to every being; ishq, the longing that burns; ren, care that starts at home. Notice which one stays; there's no right answer. When it's clear, name it silently. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words.

878.title: Love close
878.howItsDone: Traditions keep love through practice: Christians through service and prayer, Buddhists through loving-kindness meditation and small daily good deeds, and friends and families by saying it out loud.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different loves: agape, bhakti, metta, ishq and ren, each pointing its own way. Your line was many loves.

A philosopher's ladder. A myth about humans split in two. A widow on a dusty road, refusing to turn back. A basin of water and a towel. A mother guarding her only child. A coat by the door that nobody can bring themselves to move. This block of sixty days opened with a handful of words for love and a question: one thing, or many? Before the hills turn to something new, look back once. Today: Diotima.
screen: `A LADDER. A ROAD. A TOWEL.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON LOVE.` → `LOOK BACK ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the philosophers. In Plato's Symposium, Diotima teaches that love climbs, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Aristotle calls a friend another self. Montaigne, asked why he loved his friend, could only say: because it was he, because it was I. Second, the scriptures. Ruth, to her mother-in-law Naomi: “whither thou goest, I will go.” Jesus kneels and washes his friends' feet. A letter of John puts it in three words: “God is love.” In the Qur'an, one of God's names is the Loving. Third, the small. Thérèse of Lisieux and her little way: the smallest actions, done for love. The Dhammapada's water-pot, filled drop by drop. The letter of James: “swift to hear, slow to speak.” Simone Weil, holding that attention is a rare and pure kind of generosity. Fourth, the turn these sixty days kept making. Again and again, the texts treated love less as a feeling that happens to you and more as something done: keeping a friendship from fading, listening without fixing, letting a grown child go, sitting with grief, writing the note. The traditions disagree about a great deal, and their loves stay different, as yesterday showed. But the texts kept coming back to hands and feet: a towel, a road, a cup of water, a word said out loud. Love, in these sixty days, has mostly been a verb.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who hasn't heard it from you lately, maybe someone you'd never think to tell, and let their face come clear. Let the words form as plainly as you'd say them: I love you, or, if that isn't how your family talks, the version that is, like thanks for being you, or I think about you. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.

Your line: love is the practice. Tomorrow, the hills turn to work. See you there.

879.title: Most of our waking hours
879.hook: traditions have plenty to say about work, the place so much of life happens
879.howItsDone: Traditions bring faith into daily work in their own ways: some Hindus practice karma yoga, offering action without clinging to its results, and some Christians follow Brother Lawrence's practice of the presence of God during ordinary tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed sixty days on love, with Diotima's ladder among them. Your line was love is the practice.

An alarm before it's light. A commute, or a walk from the bed to the kitchen table. Then the hours: the shift, the inbox, the diapers, the field, the classroom, the delivery route, the dishes. Tally the waking hours of a week and see where they go. If the answer is work, paid or unpaid, then work is where a life is mostly lived. And if the great questions only show up in the quiet hours, they'll miss most of the day. Today begins sixty days on work. First: karma yoga.
screen: `AN ALARM. A SHIFT. THE DISHES.` → `WHERE DO THE HOURS GO?` → `SIXTY DAYS ON WORK.`

segments.voice: Start where the last block ended. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran has a plowman ask about work, and the answer bridges love and labor in five words: “Work is love made visible.” Bake bread without care, Gibran says, and you bake a bitter bread that feeds only half a hunger. The care goes in with the flour. Second, the Bhagavad Gita. On a battlefield, the warrior Arjuna wants to lay down his bow and walk away from what he's been given to do. Krishna answers that his concern is with the action alone, never with its fruits. Hindu teachers call this karma yoga: doing the work fully, while letting go of how it turns out. Third, a kitchen. A lay brother in a French monastery, remembered as Brother Lawrence, worked among pots and pans. In the letters and conversations gathered after him, he says he felt as close to God in the clatter of the kitchen as on his knees at prayer. Fourth, what these voices share, without becoming one voice. None treats work as the thing that gets in the way of a spiritual life. Gibran sees love in it. The Gita sees a path. Brother Lawrence sees God's presence. They differ on what work is for, but each puts the great questions where the hours actually go. Next come Jewish and Christian voices: a garden, sweat, a sabbath, a craftsman, an ant.

segments.voice: Choose one task you do so often you've stopped seeing it, folding laundry, packing a lunch, opening the store, and walk through it slowly in your mind as if watching a stranger: the hands, the tools, the small decisions. Then follow it outward to whoever eats, wears or uses what you do, and notice one thing about it you'd stopped noticing. If you pray, you can offer that work in your own tradition's words.

880.title: Tend and keep
880.hook: the first human is put in the garden to dress it and keep it (Genesis 2:15)
880.carry: ours to grow, and ours to guard
880.howItsDone: Some Jewish and Christian readers point to Genesis 2:15 when they speak of work as care, and some communities read it as a call to look after the earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was karma yoga: doing the work fully, and letting go of how it turns out. Your line was the work is here.

Before the serpent, before the fruit, before anyone hides among the trees, there's already a job. Genesis tells it this way: “And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.” Not to sit on a throne. Not to rest forever in the shade. To dress it, and to keep it. In this story, work arrives before anything goes wrong. Today: shamar.
screen: `BEFORE THE SERPENT.` → `A JOB IN THE GARDEN.` → `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: First, the order. Earlier in the same chapter, before the man is formed, the earth waits, because, the text says, “there was not a man to till the ground.” The garden needs a gardener. So when work gets talked about as a punishment, Genesis two answers quietly: the work came first. The hard part comes tomorrow, in chapter three. Second, dress it. In older English, to dress a garden is to work it: to dig and prune and water and weed. It's the hands-in-the-dirt verb, the one that makes things grow. Third, keep it. To keep, here, is to guard and watch over. In the King James text the same verb turns up in the priestly blessing: “The LORD bless thee, and keep thee.” Some readers note that the Hebrew behind both is the same guarding word, shamar. So the keeping asked of the gardener echoes the keeping the blessing asks of God. The gardener isn't only a laborer, but a guardian. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary workday. Put the two verbs side by side and they make a picture of care. In this story the garden isn't the gardener's to use up. It's the gardener's to make grow and to protect. Some Jewish and Christian readers have drawn from this verse a way of thinking about the earth, and about anything put into human hands: a job, a child, a row of tomatoes, a team that depends on you. Some of it is ours to grow, some ours to guard, and often the same thing asks for both.
screen: `WORK BEFORE ANYTHING GOES WRONG.` · `DRESS IT: MAKE IT GROW.` · `KEEP IT: GUARD AND WATCH OVER.` · `CARE, NOT USING UP.` · then, large: `TEND AND KEEP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing in your care, a plant, a pet, a bike, a friendship gone quiet, and look at it the way a gardener looks at a row. Ask what it needs to grow or work well, water, a repair, a call, and that's the dressing; then ask what it needs protecting from, neglect, rushing, a careless hand, and that's the keeping. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words.

881.title: Honest sweat
881.hook: in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread (Genesis 3:19)
881.howItsDone: Some Christians hear words from Genesis 3:19 on Ash Wednesday as ashes are marked on their foreheads, and Jewish and Christian readers turn to this chapter and to Psalm 128 when they speak of the dignity of hard work.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shamar, to guard and watch over: a job in the garden before anything went wrong. Your line was ours to grow, and ours to guard.
screen: `OURS TO GROW, AND OURS TO GUARD.`

segments.voice: Thorns. A field that fights back. In Genesis chapter three, after the fruit, the ground changes. The man is told it will bring forth thorns and thistles. Then comes a line that sounds like every long shift, every harvest, every back that aches by evening: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.” The garden of chapter two had a gardener. Now the gardener sweats. Today: honest sweat.
screen: `THORNS AND THISTLES.` → `A FIELD THAT FIGHTS BACK.` → `IN THE SWEAT OF THY FACE.`

segments.voice: First, read closely. In the King James text, the word cursed lands on the ground: “cursed is the ground for thy sake.” The job from chapter two isn't canceled. What changes is the resistance: thorns, thistles, soil that won't cooperate. Some readers hear punishment here. Some hear a plain description of the world as it is, where good things take effort. Both readings stay close to the words. Second, sweat, then bread. The verse ties the two together: effort, and then food on the table. There's a quiet dignity in that order. Bread in this story isn't handed down from the sky. It's earned with the body. Third, the rest of the verse is sobering: “till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” The worker is made of the same ground he works. On Ash Wednesday, some Christians hear words drawn from this verse as ashes are marked on their foreheads. Fourth, sweat doesn't stay bitter everywhere in the Bible. A psalm says of the one who walks in God's ways: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.” The same hands, the same labor, and now happiness. Put chapter three and that psalm side by side, and honest sweat looks like this: tired arms, real bread, and a day spent on something that fed someone.
screen: `CURSED IS THE GROUND, NOT THE JOB.` · `SWEAT, THEN BREAD.` · `DUST TO DUST.` · `PSALM 128: THE HAPPY LABORER.` · then, large: `HONEST SWEAT.`

segments.voice: Feel your body as a working thing, shoulders, forearms, hands, and notice what it has carried this week: groceries, a child, a box, a keyboard for too many hours. 882.title: Six days, then stop
882.hook: six days shalt thou labor, but the seventh is a sabbath (Exodus 20:9–10)
882.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat mark it from Friday evening to Saturday night, lighting candles and setting the day apart from work; Christians who keep Sunday call it the Lord's day, while Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was honest sweat: a field that fights back, and bread earned with the body. Your line was tired arms, real bread.

A list that never ends. Answer one message and two more arrive. Clear the sink and it's full again by evening. Work, left to itself, has no edge. So the Ten Commandments draw one: “Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God.” Work, and then a wall across the week, the same wall for everyone. Today: six days.
screen: `A LIST THAT NEVER ENDS.` → `WORK HAS NO EDGE.` → `SO THE COMMANDMENT DRAWS ONE.`

segments.voice: First, notice both halves. The commandment doesn't only say stop. It says labor, six days, and do all thy work. Work and rest arrive as one command, two sides of a single rhythm. Second, notice who gets to stop. The verse keeps going: “thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.” The rest isn't a perk for the owner. The servant stops. The cattle stop. The outsider stops. Rest here is a kind of fairness, written into the week. Third, the reasons. In Exodus, the reason is creation: God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh. When the commandments are given again in Deuteronomy, the reason changes: “remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt.” People who once worked without end are told to build a week that ends. Fourth, how it's kept. Jews who keep Shabbat mark it from Friday evening to Saturday night, with candles, a meal, and a day set apart from work. Christians who keep Sunday call it the Lord's day, while Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. The shapes differ. The edge is the point. And at the end of a week, a look back: a thread on a wrist, many loves, love as a practice, then work. Where the hours go. A garden to tend and keep. Honest sweat. And now the stop that keeps it all human.
screen: `WORK AND REST, ONE COMMAND.` · `THE STOP IS FOR EVERYONE.` · `CREATION, THEN EGYPT: TWO REASONS.` · `THE EDGE IS THE POINT.` · then, large: `SIX DAYS, THEN STOP.`

segments.voice: Picture the shape of your coming week, the shifts, the deadlines, the people waiting on you, and look for an edge: not a whole day if that isn't possible, but an evening, a morning, a few hours. Picture what you'd put down, the laptop, the phone, the list, then ask the commandment's second question: who else could stop with you? If you pray, you can hold that stopping time in your own tradition's words.
Six days. From the Ten Commandments: six days of work, then a seventh set apart, for everyone within the gates. Today's word.
Your line: fairness, written into the week. The rest belongs to everyone within the gates. Day eight hundred eighty-two, done.
